utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning everybody in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Good morning to everyone. May we have the appearances today, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Tom Hannis, Belinda Pidwell, and Crispian Smith for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Cvijetic and Deirdre Montgomery for the Stanisic Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Dragan Krgovic, Igor Pantelic, Aleksandar Aleksic, and Daniella Sinobad appearing for Zupljanin Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. May we have the witness back to the stand, if there is nothing that we need divert our attention to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Miskovic, good morning to you. I remind you, sir, that you're still on your oath. Yes, Ms. Pidwell.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It doesn't work.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Is it working now?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's working.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Sir, on Friday, we -- we ended by looking at a document which were the minutes of the Municipal Board meeting which was held on the 23rd of April, 1992. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And there was a reference in that document to a meeting which was scheduled to take place two days later at Cirkin Polje.

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Did you attend that meeting at Cirkin Polje on Saturday, the 25th of April?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did. I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Who was present at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, according to the agenda, there was the commander of the TO, Kuruzovic; and the chief of the MUP, Simo Drljaca; as well as the representatives of the Serb authorities of the Serbian municipality of the Prijedor, that is, the -- the highest ranking people, Mico Kovacevic, Slavisa Dakic, and others.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, Mico Stakic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And do you recall the decisions that were made at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember. Since there was the danger of continued confrontation in Prijedor municipality, in order to prevent the conflicts, it was decided to seize power. And it was agreed that this would take place at 4.00 a.m., and it was done that way, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And how was it decided on which day this takeover would take place?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke about that earlier. On that day, the 29th, I was at a meeting in Prijedor at the MUP. The representatives of the SDA were there, the political representatives, and the representatives of the authorities. Mujadzic and the president of the municipality, whose name I always forget. And there was the chief of the MUP, Telundzic. And it was a friendly conversation until the communications clerk brought a dispatch and read it out to all of us and the dispatch said that the Muslim forces were attacking barracks, intercepting our armoured vehicles. And then among the police officers present at the meeting, there was a commotion, but we were able to calm them. After the meeting, I was invited to come to the barracks, and I did. Everybody was sitting there, Kuruzovic and ... Kuruzovic, the TO commander; then Simo, the chief of the MUP; and Jankovic. Furthermore, Cadzo; Arsic, the barracks commander of the 43rd Brigade; and his deputy, Beljaja; as well as Radovan Arsic -- Arsic's deputy were already there. As far as I remember, these were the people who were already there when I arrived. The decision was taken then to take over power with regard to the events mentioned in the dispatch because they were what prompted us to do so. And it was agreed to do it on the same evening. That was Arsic's proposal. But I was afraid that there could be a conflict, because it was a workday, and I was afraid that things might take a bad turn. So my idea was to do it on Saturday, and as they said to me, Simo -- but from whom do you take power on Saturday, because it isn't a working day? So the final decision was to do it in the evening, that is, the night from the 29th through the 30th, and it was done that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Going back, sir, to the meeting that was held on the 25th of April, was a decision made at that meeting as to when the takeover would take place?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That decision wasn't taken then. If you followed the development of events, in all documents and all contacts and conversations there was always the language, if the Serb People in Prijedor municipality should be threatened, then there would be takeover of power, according to Variant B. You can find that in the text, Variant B. And if you allow, and if it's of interest, let me explain that the fear among the Serb People was not irrational. So I could give you a historic overview of events that triggered this apprehension and fear.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Well, sir, we don't have the benefit of that much time. Let me --

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was just a question.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Let me take you back. Were there any additional meetings between the 25th of April and the 29th of April, when you attended this meeting at the MUP building in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, from today's vantage point, after 20 years, I couldn't be certain about either. I don't remember that, but I remember that meeting, so if you could remind me, I will -- you'll probably jog my memory.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: When you attended the meeting at the MUP building, what was the purpose of the meeting?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't really remember what the purpose of the meeting was because I arrived late. Everybody was already there. Police officers and these representatives and everybody. Only later did my guys from the municipality tell me to go to that meeting, and they had gone to that other meeting which -- of which I wasn't aware then. So I don't know what the purpose of the meeting was.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Who chaired the meeting at the MUP building?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The chief did, Telundzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And who was there representing the SDA?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mirza Mujadzic did, and the president of the Municipal Assembly who was elected on behalf of the SDA. I always forget his name.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And how were you informed about the subsequent meeting held by the Serb municipal leaders?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I came back from the meeting, they called me up and told me to go to the barracks, which I did. And there, everybody was already there, as I have already explained.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And you told us who was present at this -- the second meeting, and you mentioned Simo. Who were you referring to when you used that --

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Simo Drljaca. Because that earlier meeting, I remember, there was the Committee for Internal Organisation when he was appointed to be chief of the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And where did the second meeting take place exactly?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean with the representatives of the Serb authorities to which I came late? Do you mean that one?

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... yes.

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the JNA barracks in Prijedor. At Urije.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And you've told us that a decision was made there and then to take over the municipality that evening. Were you -- what arrangements were --

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the following day. That is, the following night.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: What actual arrangements were decided upon then to take over the municipality?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing special was decided upon. The TO, which was in existence already, and the police, the Serb police, were supposed to prepare the manpower to perform the takeover, to carry out -- to -- and the institutions should be prepared, and there should be a certain number of people available.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Did you decide to meet later on that evening?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, at 2.00 a.m. We -- we were supposed to consider -- or to assess whether everything was well-organised and whether we should carry out the operation. So we were supposed to check whether everything was we well-prepared and likely to succeed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And did you, in fact, meet again at 2.00 a.m.?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Where did that meeting take place?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It took place at Cirkin Polje on the premises of the local commune. Kuruzovic, the commander of the TO, reported to us that everything that was functioning well and that there shouldn't be any problems. Simo reported in respect of the police that everything was well-organised and that there shouldn't be any problems. And when all that was said, the decision was taken that the takeover of power should be carried out at 4.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: So what happened between 2.00 a.m. and 4.00 a.m. on this night?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, from 4.00 a.m. till 6.00 a.m., all institutions in the cities were taken over by these formations; that is, the MUP, the municipality, the SDK, the post-office, and so on. And I must point out that there were no problems, no excessive events, and nobody got as much as scratched in the operation, and -- which was a big relief for all of us.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Sir, before -- before the actual takeover took place at 4.00 a.m., was -- was there a gathering of -- of people, of army and police, at any particular point?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I explained already that there was no rally at the staff. The Serb police was there, and there was the TO commander; and the chief of the police reported to us that they had mobilized the manpower and prepared everything to carry out the operation. And once they had done that, the decision was taken at 2.00 that the operation should be launched at 4.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: During the -- this period of the takeover, where were you based?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was on the premises of the local commune where the decision was taken. I stayed there all the time on duty-service by the telephone, because I had grown up there and my colleagues were involved and they were all armed. But once I heard that everything had gone smoothly, I really was relieved.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: So when you say you were on duty-service by the telephone, who was reporting in to you at this time?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't the operative officer. But I wanted to know. I was nervous and apprehensive. That's why I sat by the telephone all the time, to hear what -- what they had to say, if anybody would call. I was especially interested in the police because of my colleagues. And those who carried out the takeover of power were also my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And how did you hear that the takeover had been successful?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, reports were submitted. Kuruzovic and Simo Drljaca informed everybody, and they reported on what they had done. They said that they had problems with the guard at the SDK who was asleep. They had trouble waking him. And that was the last facility that was taken over.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: I'd like you to have a look at a document, sir. It's 65 ter 411, tab 19.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: You'll see, sir, this is a dispatch dated the 30th of April from Simo Drljaca to the Banja Luka CSB. And it says: "Based on your dispatch of the above number and date, please be informed ... ten police stations and 1.587 policemen were mobilized."

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Does that -- does that figure seem correct to you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it is correct. But that was a dispatch that was sent through police channels. I wasn't familiar with it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the volume in the witness's headphones please be lowered.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's too high.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Sir, do you remember giving an interview on the radio about the takeover of the municipality in April 1995?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember. There was an announcement. I spoke for the radio on behalf of the people who were taking over the power.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Turn to 65 ter 587, please. It's tab 60.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Do you recall listening to the audio version of this interview last week?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I also read this -- yes, these were my words, the words I spoke on the Radio Prijedor broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: So you recognised your voice; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And the context.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: If we turn to the second page, please, in both versions.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: At the end of your speech, sir, you'll see the reporter makes an announcement that that was Mr. Simo Drljaca.

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see that. That was a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Was Mr. Simo Drljaca involved in this interview at all?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he was, but I really can't remember. I can't remember Slobodan being there. But having read here that he was, I remember. That was 20 years ago.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: In any event, the first speaker that we see on this transcript was you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was me; that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And the next speaker, did you recognise the voice of Slobodan Kuruzovic?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes -- yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And did you also recognise the voice of Mico Kovacevic?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And your account of the -- the takeover during that radio broadcast, was that an accurate account?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, 99 per cent of it was accurate. One must take into account that we were emotional at the time and the desire to show that the operation was done well. Am I too close? Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: I'd ask for that transcript to be admitted and marked, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1617, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: After the takeover had occurred during the night, did you inform anyone of the events and the outcome?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no one to inform. I didn't inform anyone. Well, at least as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And after the takeover, did you, in your capacity as SDS president, visit the municipal buildings that day to see who was now in power for yourself?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, that evening when the decision was made to take over power, another decision was reached, namely, that representatives of Serbs that were in charge of certain positions within the Municipal Assembly, Stakic was the president of the Assembly, the secretary, the Executive Committee president, that they should show up at their work at 6.00 a.m. so that by 7.00 a.m. they would already be there. And the entrance policeman, I think, was placed, who prevented the president of the municipality to enter the building. And someone else, I think, some other officials who were members of the SDA. Everyone else was at their workplace, as usual.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And do you recall how it was announced to the people of Prijedor that the takeover had, in fact, taken place?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I have mentioned a moment ago, before this interview and after the takeover of power, an announcement was read over the radio to the citizens with explanations of why the takeover had taken place, and that the situation is calm, that there will be no repression or any problems, that president of municipality and some officials were replaced, others remained working. That was the gist of the announcement. It preceded the interview for the radio. It was repeated on several occasions.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And after the takeover, did the weekly meetings of the Municipal Assembly continue?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the authorities worked within the building of the Municipal Assembly. According to Variant B, they started working independently. The activities within the party were frozen, and the government functioned normally. Of course, there were problems and fears, and therefore there were regular meetings, contacts with the citizens, with representatives of other ethnicities, and it went on for a month, until the said events. Check-points were set up that were organised in 1991 so that, for instance, somebody wouldn't go into areas where there were a majority of the other ethnicity group and caused some excessive events, but there were no problems in that period.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Who manned these check-points?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police. We had the police doing it, and they had their own check-points in order to prevent somebody going to the other side and causing some problems. That was the main reason for setting up the check-points, to prevent some individuals or groups from doing something unforeseeable. And we didn't have any problems, neither in the period before the takeover, nor after it, all the way until this attack on Prijedor and the said events that followed it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Can we look at another document. It's 65 ter 413. It's tab 21. We might need the B/C/S a little larger, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: You'll see, sir, a document in front of you which is the minutes of the 2nd Session of the National Defence Council of the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor held on the --

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And you were present?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yeah, I can see. I don't remember it, but I can see here in the minutes that I was there.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Firstly, could you explain to us who this body is, the National Defence Council?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The National Defence Council, well, that was a type of organisation that was taken over from the previous period, from the period of socialist government. It was a provisional organ, and it was tasked with helping the Municipal Assembly and the president of the Assembly in issues related to security. This system existed in former Yugoslavia, and we maintained it after the takeover. As you can see, there was discussion about mobilization here. The decision was reached first, and then there were discussions about how to implement them.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And if we can turn to the next page, please. I think, actually, the B/C/S, if you can remain on the same page; and the English, we turn to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Under number 6, we see that a curfew was to be introduced.

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that took place.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And under number 7, we see that it states: "All paramilitary units and individuals who possess weapons and ammunition illegally are called upon to surrender them immediately, and not later than 11 May ... to the public security station in Prijedor." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can -- I see that. I remember them, both of these.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And why was it necessary to make a decision on the surrender of weapons by the 11th of May?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, in relation to the curfew, it was introduced to make sure that in the night hours when it was dark, would not - and I mean either an individual or a group - would cause some kind of problems on any of the sides. That was the main motive for the curfew. And this item about paramilitary units and individuals who illegally possess weapons, they're being asked to surrendered them to the legal authorities, the police. Again, for the same purpose: To make sure that there will be no armed fighting or anything like that. You have seen that throughout the period within the municipality of Prijedor there were no paramilitary formations nor were there any problematic events.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Well, sir, if there were no paramilitary formations or problematic events, why was it necessary to issue a direction to surrender weapons at this time?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is stated here. If there were any. If there are individuals who are in possession of illegal arms. This is what is stated here. They should hand them over. Those who had authorisation from the MUP to possess arms, they didn't have to surrender their arms.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: I seek to tender that document, those minutes, at this stage, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1618, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: If we can go to 65 ter 415, please. It's tab 24.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: You'll see on your screen, sir, we have some minutes of the SDS Municipal Board on the 9th of May, 1992, with you presiding. Do you recall this meeting?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just read this. Could you please enlarge it a little bit for me?

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: There's a reference there, sir, under the number 2, afterwards it goes on and says: "Go on with the talks observing all the properties [sic], but always keep in mind the final goal. The idea is to achieve everything peacefully and without destruction." What was it meant when it said "go on with the talks observing all the properties [sic]"? Sorry, "proprieties."

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Nothing special happened. I don't know what the idea was. I cannot explain this.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: If we can turn to the next page where Simo Drljaca is reporting. Page 2 on each, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me just find him. I can't find him. Oh, yes, there he is.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And Mr. Drljaca is saying that there's a problem with the protection of the facilities and "it's imperative that the TO take over such details so that the police can go back to their duties."

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Well, that's logical. The question was who will be providing security for the already-present facilities in order to avoid any problems. And that was something that Territorial Defence and police had to take care of. And Simo is here suggesting that TO should be doing that because they have more manpower. It says here that they were afraid of crime.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And he goes on to discuss the negotiations with the Ljubija and Kozarac stations and a deadline being extended. What was that deadline for?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, after the takeover in Prijedor, the police stations in Ljubija and Kozarac were not taken over. They continued functioning in their areas. And then there were talks between them for the purpose of resubordinating them to the new-formed MUP Prijedor, under the new circumstances, and that's the context of this conversation.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: So those -- those police stations and areas that they covered, Ljubija and Kozarac, they were Muslim areas, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, yes. Croats were also in Ljubija. The majority of Croats lived in the area of Ljubija.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Why was it necessary to carry out full mobilisation of the TO and the reserve police force within that context?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had already been mobilized at the time of the takeover of power, both the Territorial Defence and the police. This is just continuing -- continuation of their functioning. There were no new mobilisations of the Territorial Defence and the police. They were mobilized before the takeover of power, and then they continued functioning like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: I'd ask that that document be admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1619, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Now, sir, during the month of May, were you involved in negotiations which took place with the inhabitants of Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that one-month period, until the attack of Muslim forces against Prijedor, many talks were held with representatives of Kozarac and other local communes, individuals, and groups, with the goal of finding the best solution that would exclude any problems taking place in the municipality of Prijedor. One can see that in every document. One can see that through everything conversation.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Besides you, who else was involved in these negotiations?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, me, Stakic, Drljaca, Mico, one of us or several of us together. Kuruzovic was also involved a lot.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And who were you negotiating with?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Savunovic [phoen] also. All the people from the top levels of government were involved in the talks, either individually or in groups of two, three. It depends.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And from the -- from the people of Kozarac, who were you negotiating with?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had a delegation. As far as I remember, it was a math teacher, Mujkanovic I think his name was. I know where his house was in Krkici [phoen]. And there was a group of people with him. They came for the talks on that occasion. In the period prior to the takeover, we were arranging the arrival of me and Mujadzic to Kozarac, and it almost took place; however, it didn't. Later on I was told by some friends of mine from Kozarac that this arrival of ours was postponed because there was a chance that an extremist group would make an attempt on our lives. But that is only something I heard after the take over of power. Now whether that's true or not, I don't know, but that's whey heard from the people of Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And could you briefly summarize for the Trial Chamber what it was exactly that you were negotiating?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The basic negotiations were about security, on one hand; and on the other hand, the issue of changing of emblems on people's uniforms. The flags should have been placed. And the third thing was disarmament. Those were the three topics of the agenda, these three segments.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And at some point was a deadline imposed for the people of Kozarac to surrender their weapons?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you. I know that, like this: I did not personally set any deadlines on behalf of the party. It was the government, the police, and the army who were in charge of that. Disarmament is part of their domain. The government functioned, and they took over all the tasks of the government, as we have seen in the documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Do you recall why it was that these negotiations came to an end?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I know is that the negotiations just failed to produce a final resolution of issues related to these three segments, and I think that's why the negotiations didn't come through.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And after the negotiations failed, what action was taken against Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember. If you could remind me ...

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Did you -- were you aware that the town of Kozarac was shelled?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot remember. I assume -- I do know that it was shelled, but I think that took place only after the attack on Prijedor, not in this 30-day period between the 30th of April and the 30th of May. I don't think it took place then - the shelling, I mean - while the negotiations were going on, because part of the negotiation was a decision, joint decision, whereby the army was put in charge of security on the roads. That was a joint position taken by all the parties.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Did you actually go into -- or into the town of Kozarac during the month of May?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, no, I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Where did these negotiations take place?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the premises of Prijedor municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And do you recall the last date of the negotiations or when they failed --

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, at least. No, that, I don't remember. That was a long time ago, 20 years ago.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: When did you go back to Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the first time? For the first time, it was after the shelling. I think I reached Dera. And not again for a long time.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And this was -- this was a town that you knew well. What you did see when you arrived there, after the shelling?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I saw some houses and buildings destroyed by the shelling.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And were the people of Kozarac going about their daily business?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't see that because I only passed through the main street. I think it was called Mladen Stojanovic Street. That's the only part of the town that I saw. Whether people went about their daily business elsewhere, I don't know. I didn't go anywhere else.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: I want you to have a look at the document, sir, which is 65 ter 422.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Sorry, just bear with me. No, 420.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: These are some minutes of another National Defence Council meeting, this time on the 15th of May, with you being present and Mr. -- Dr. Stakic presiding.

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And if we turn to the next page, please, on both versions.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Just before the heading "Conclusions," you'll see this. It states there, simply: "Disarmament of Paramilitary Formations" as a topic. And then the persons who participated in the discussion about that: Drljaca, Zeljaja, a number of other people. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean item 4, disarming paramilitary formations, yes, I can see that. Simo Drljaca, Radmilo Zeljaja, and others took part in the discussion. Conclusions were adopted. All these are members of the government. Zeljaja represented the garrison. There was somebody from the National Defence. Bosko, Mandic, and Ranko Travar were members of the defence council. The entire -- the entire set.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Sir, you've told us previously that there were no paramilitary formations -- no Serb paramilitary formations in the municipality at this time?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: So what did this relate -- what did this relate to, then?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most probably it related to the paramilitary units on the Muslim and Croat side.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: I ask that that document be admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1620, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You will remember that ...

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Could we now have 65 ter 422 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Here we have, sir, some minutes of the Municipal Board of the SDS meeting held on the 18th of May, with you opening and chairing the meeting.

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And if we go down to the bottom of the page, we'll see --

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: -- some conclusions that were adopted, after some discussion. And one of them was: "Disarm paramilitary units and citizens owning [sic] weapons by peaceful means until the end of May; after that time, force will be used to enforce the disarmament." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see that. Item 2, to disarm paramilitary units and citizens who are in possession of weapons by peaceful means; later on, force will be used. Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And are you aware that all the paramilitary units and citizens owning weapons were in fact disarmed, or did it come to the position where force was used?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when we're talking about paramilitary units, I'd like to note - and we have already discussed this before the beginning of trial - I had heard that in the area of Carakovo, which is a Muslim local Muslim commune, there was a paramilitary unit of Green Berets headed by Slavko Ecimovic. I was surprised to hear that because I knew the man and I could never picture him in that role. And I asked Dr. Sadikovic, who knew Ecimovic, to go and ask him to come for talks. And he, indeed, did that and came back to me and said, Simo, there's nothing doing. He has ammunition belts across his chest and automatic rifle and he's playing Rambo. I was very surprised to hear that because the man was an acquaintance of mine; I knew him; he was a businessman; he liked good living; and I was really shocked by the news of his transformation. And that means, any way, that there were paramilitary units on the other side that needed to be disarmed. And later on, in Prijedor, this Slavko showed up with his unit. And you can see that all that's discussed here was indeed justified.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: I seek to admit that document at this stage, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1621, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Sir, I want to now ask you some questions about your visit to the detention facility at Omarska.

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: When were you first told that a delegation was coming from Banja Luka to visit this detention facility?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was never told about that, and I didn't know about it. I just saw by chance on the pavement outside the municipal building when this delegation came in a motorcade, and I think Mico Stakic was there, and Drljaca went to accompany them, and they said to me, Come along. And that's how I came to go to Omarska with them. I had no prior information this visit would take place. I, as the president of the party, did not take part in the government after the takeover. Party functions were frozen. But I went everywhere, I dropped by the town hall, the municipal building, other institutions. I just -- I was just passing time.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: So who was part of the delegation? You've said Stakic and Drljaca accompanied them, but who was it that came from Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mico was there too, not only Drljaca. I don't know who came from Banja Luka. I only saw them when they came out of the cars in Omarska. There was president of the municipal, Radic; I believe there was Vojo Kupresanin, Stojan Zupljanin; I believe also Radoslav Brdjanin. That is it. I may be mistaken about one of them. Maybe not all of these were present. Maybe I omitted someone. But that's all I can tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just to clarify, perhaps the witness should be asked: When he says Mico, whom does he mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mico Kovacevic - I'm sorry I'm using his first name; we were on very good terms; we were next door neighbours living on the same street - when I say Mico, I mean Mico Kovacevic. I know it's very important for the Court to use the first and last name.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Right. So we -- you joined -- you joined this delegation, and --

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: -- from Prijedor town hall or the municipal building --

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. No, in fact, they were already on the way. They did not get out of the car to go into the municipal building. They were on the road already. And these two were on the side of the road. Maybe they had already arranged it by telephone.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: So you went into a vehicle with -- well, with who?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. With Mico and Stakic and Simo. I think even that there was -- that was a police vehicle, but I'm not sure. I would not like to make a mistake here. Anyway, I went there.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And did they tell you what the purpose of the visit was?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not really. We just got into the car and went. They said, We're going to Omarska, the investigating centre -- the investigation centre. That's what they told me.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And were you aware at this point in time that Omarska was being used for what you call an investigation centre?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was the information I had; namely, that a rather large number of persons were held in Omarska, being subjected to operative investigation conducted by public and state security personnel. And as a professional, following that logic, I believed, and I still believe, that it was an investigation centre where people were supposed to be investigated to establish their possible criminal liability, and those who were not charged with anything were supposed to be released. I'm speaking as a professional.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Were you involved in the decision to use the premises of Omarska as an investigation centre?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I don't even know when that decision was made.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: When you arrived at Omarska with this delegation, what did you see?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we came in -- this was the door, and then we passed by one building, and then stopped within the compound, facing another building. In the first building outside which we stopped, there is a staircase leading upstairs. We got out there, climbed the steps, and entered the conference hall on the first floor. In the building next to us that was fenced in - the fence was there even before the war, before the takeover - there were a number of citizens of Prijedor, rather a large number of citizens, whom I knew. But since they had not shaven for a long time, I couldn't recognise them. But they certainly could recognise me, so I was rather embarrassed. I kept my head down. And keeping my head down, I went into the building.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And besides being unshaven, what was the -- what did the detainees generally look like, in terms of their state of health and appearance?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know what? You -- you don't need explaining. Of course, if they didn't shave for a long time, they had long beards. If they hadn't changed clothes for a long time and hadn't washed them, you know what it's like. I'm here only for a couple of days and I still had to have my shirts washed. And they were all crumpled because they slept in the same clothes, they couldn't hang them properly for the night. That's whey meant. About the health, I don't know who was in what state of health and who had what kind of health problems, whether those problems, if any occurred there or whether they came with these same problems. The physicians who examined them know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I apologise because I think that there is one part of his response, on the page 25 line 2 or 3, missing. It was related to the -- some video recordings. He mentioned that. It's not ...

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: The witness did say - he's speaking very fast: I was keeping my head down coming into the building, and that is how you see me on that video footage.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: You've told us that you saw a large number of people at Omarska on this day and that you knew a lot of them. What was their ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Muslims and Croats, both. Except there were more Muslims, because, generally, there is a larger percentage of Muslims in the municipality of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And what -- what took place at the -- at the meeting room on the first floor? You've told us you went in, you walked upstairs, and went into a meeting room. What took place there?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that meeting, somebody representing this facility reported on the situation within the facility, on the steps and measures they had taken, on their intention to file charges possibly against individuals. That's --

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... who was that -- sorry, who was that person?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know the name. But you can probably see it on that video footage. It must have been the director of that investigation centre. The warden. The film shows the entire course of that visit.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Yes, we'll have a look at that in a minute. How long did this -- did this meeting take place?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As best as I can remember, not more than an hour, an hour and a half, perhaps. Perhaps I could have given you a better answer in 1991 or 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Was everyone who had arrived with you, in terms of the delegation, present at this meeting that took place?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We were all there. We came into the room together.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And were questions asked of the -- the person who was convening this meeting?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you that. Not after all this time. I don't remember. I think it was just the briefing by that warden. Or perhaps there were some questions asked, but I really can't remember. Possibly. Possibly, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And, sir, were you surprised at all by what you saw there on that day?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know in what sense you mean. "Surprised." I was taken aback by the appearance of the people I saw there, because I had seen them before looking differently. That's one thing. And another thing is that I was unable to recognise them when they looked like that. And I have already answered to you concerning my professional point of view on -- on that investigation centre. It all looked rather legitimate and legal, the way it was done.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And after that meeting, did you go directly back to the vehicles, or did you have a walk around the other buildings at Omarska?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We got back into the vehicles immediately. We did not even tour that building. It was just next to the building which we entered. The two buildings were not far apart, 10 metres perhaps. And all these people were standing up as we were passing.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Did you ask to -- to talk to any of the people who were being detained there?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was a police investigation. I did not interfere.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Do you recall when this visit took place?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember that either. It was a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Can we have a look at a document, please. It's 65 ter 1566.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Ms. Pidwell, we're just near the break. We may as well wait until we return. So we return in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Pidwell, you were about to show a document to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Sir, while that document is being brought up on the screen, just to clarify, did you go to Omarska at any other time during the summer of 1992 or just on one occasion?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the one and only time. I never went there either before or afterward.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Are you familiar with this newspaper that you see on your screen?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a local paper, "Kozarski Vjesnik."

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And do you see the -- the heading on the left -- the main heading on the left-hand side of your screen, which says new authorities -- sorry, which says: "Krajina representatives in Prijedor"?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There's a heading above that which reads: "Visits." But the main heading is "Krajina representatives in Prijedor."

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And perhaps if we could make a little bit -- yes, that portion, exactly, a little bit larger for the witness. And we see that this newspaper is reporting on a visit from representatives from the Autonomous Region of Krajina - Brdjanin, Vukic, Zupljanin, Radic - saying they had visited Prijedor on Wednesday. Do you recall whether this coincided with your visit with these men to Omarska or do you think this was a different visit?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know of any other visit. I know that when I was there, there were the people whom I mentioned. I don't know about anything else. But I know that I never went to Omarska or Keraterm before or after that one occasion.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: If we could turn, please, to the fourth page in the B/C/S and the second page in the English. And in the B/C/S, if we could perhaps go to the right-hand side; it's the article on the other side of the page. Thank you. And if we could make it slightly bigger, if possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Now, I'm not sure whether you can actually read that, sir. It's a little bit blurred.

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's difficult, but I can see -- I can read the bold letters. Radoslav Brdjanin, Radoslav Vukic, Prijedor Radic, Stojan Zupljanin; these names are printed in bold letters.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And there's a portion there which says: "After they," referring to those -- the part of the delegation from Banja Luka, "had made a tour of the combat areas and collection centres, the visitors from Krajina thanked their hosts for their hospitality and efforts in creating a new Serbian state in that area." Do you -- do you agree that that's an accurate reflection of what happened during your visit, that the visitors thanked the hosts from Prijedor of their efforts after they visited the combat areas and collection centres?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you in the proofing, and I must repeat it now, that I don't know where they went earlier. That information is not known to me. They may have come from Banja Luka and waited before we entered. Or maybe they went to the combat area and then went on. That's something I don't know. I only know what I mentioned, what I spoke about. But I can see here that Ecimovic is mentioned also.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And do you recall being present when Radoslav Brdjanin said: "What we have seen in Prijedor is an example of a job well done"?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I tell you, I don't even remember who spoke up there, let alone such details. No, I really don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And you -- you told us earlier, sir, that you didn't know that this delegation was coming before you actually joined them. Why was it, then, that you joined the delegation going to Omarska?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I told you, I was on the sidewalk. And they -- the people from the municipality, that is, Mico Stakic, and maybe there was also Simo, I'm not sure, or perhaps he only drove up the car. But they were outside. I knew nothing about that. And they almost dragged me with them because there was a delegation coming, and I had to come with them. And that's how it was. I was almost dragged there. And I didn't know at all that they would come or where they would go because they arrived when I was on the pavement.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: I'd ask that that newspaper article be admitted and marked, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I object. I believe that the Prosecutor failed to show a sufficient nexus between this witness and this document. He is not familiar with the article, nor does he know anything about the statements. And he even wrongly identified the persons who went to visit Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I support Mr. Krgovic's objection. I believe that the witness's testimony is of much better quality than the article itself, so that the journalist's interpretation of the events may be superfluous at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Ms. Pidwell, I'm trying to remind myself as to where we about a year ago on this matter of newspaper articles, and my recollection is that the substance of the objections are well-founded insofar as that what we have, taken at its highest, accounts by a -- I was going to say a third person, but by somebody outside of the principles involved here and which the witness on the stand doesn't necessarily accept how -- and could -- could you assist me as to how, in your view, this is admissible and -- and of assistant?

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour. This newspaper article is dated 17th of July, 1992. The witness couldn't recall the exact date when the delegation came from Banja Luka. He says in his view it was the one and only time the delegation came and visited the collection centres in the municipality of Prijedor. This newspaper article is corroborative of his evidence that a delegation did in fact come and did go to the -- the collection centres, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... his term --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: He was there. He has given viva voce testimony as to what happened. What do we need an article for?

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: In my submission, sir, the article assists Your Honours in determining the date, the exact date of the visit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, that is not possible because the article was probably written after the visit, even a few days later. So based on the article we cannot establish the date of the visit. We can tell the date when it was published, but not when the visit took place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Do you know from another source what the date is? Because you can with this article. If the article -- the article is from 17th of July and it says that the visit was on Wednesday. Wednesday -- Wednesday before 17th of July was the 14th of July. Is there any ... do we have the -- a date for this visit from another source?

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Or is this a convenient way to determine the date?

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: This is -- in my submission, Your Honour, this is the most convenient way to determine the date of this visit, because the witness - and we have can't called all of the witnesses from Prijedor at this stage - however, 18 years later, it's very difficult for them to determine, exactly, a date. They may be able to say summer; they may be able to June, July. But it may come -- this is the date that the accused visited Omarska. And, in my submission, it is -- it's important for Your Honours to know when that occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have another problem, Your Honours. I believe that no date is stated on this article. It was admitted in the Brdjanin case, but I don't believe that there is a date indication here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Inferentially, I gather -- sorry. Yes, from -- as Judge Delvoie has said, that the -- inferentially, that the -- the date would be the Wednesday preceding the date of publication, which would make it the 14th of July. And the Chamber would admit the document for the limited purpose of establishing the date, not for the contents.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1622, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: I want to show you a video now, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: It's 65 ter 2320, at tab 48. It's in Sanction. Now, if I can just comment briefly. There is background noise and so forth in this video. It's an ITN video going to Omarska. And in the next video is actually the visit at Omarska. They're in two separate videos. I don't propose for the witness to comment on the -- the audio, which is a lot of background noise and so forth. I'm going to ask him, really, just to identify some of the individuals. So the interpreters don't need to interpret the sound as they go along.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Sir, do you recognise any of those people in that photo frame?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Do you know what they're doing?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I can see them standing, and the fat one is moving.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Okay. Let's ...

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Just while we're watching that, did you have to go through any check-points when you visited Omarska?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't remember which way we travelled there. Much time has elapsed. And check-points were nothing extraordinary, especially in areas populated by several ethnic -- ethnicities. That was the usual practice. There were countless check-points all the way to the border with Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: If we can move it up to 12:30.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Pause there.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Do you recognise that building?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: What is it?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's Keraterm, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can tell by the chimney. The chimney belongs to the brickworks. This was the building next to the brickworks. It was a modern factory which had been built some five or six years, maybe ten, before the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Do you recognise that building?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. This is the building in which I earned my pension.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And which building is that?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The MUP building in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And we see, there, a line of women. Do you know why -- did you see women lined up outside the MUP building in Prijedor in 1992?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember. I can see a line here, and the line is in front of the MUP building. They're probably waiting for some documents issued by the MUP, because the MUP also had remit over civil affairs.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And what kind of documents would -- would they be waiting for?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. But I know what the SUP [as interpreted] did. Apart of -- from operative work, there was also the civil work, such as personal identity cards, registering your domicile, registering motor cars, et cetera. That was a department of all the MUPs, including the one in Prijedor. Also driving tests to get your -- to get a driving licence.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And in order to leave the municipality, did you need to obtain some kind of document or authorisation from the MUP at this time?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you needed some document so that the authorities know that somebody had left so that they needn't search for people and that there would be no suspicion of something else having happened.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This woman is holding a personal identity card.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: All right. I think we can fast-forward now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that woman, but I can't remember her name. This one is Stakic. The one behind him is Simo.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: The one -- the one holding his arm out is ...

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is Milomir Stakic, president of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: That's at 15:45 of the tape.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And the person directly behind him in the camouflage uniform is ...

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Simo Drljaca, looking toward us, standing in the door. Yeah, he is shaking that woman's hand, the woman wearing red.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Let's pause here.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: So we have Stakic, I think, on the very left. Who's next to him, going from left to right across the table?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mico Kovacevic, president of the Executive Committee.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And next to him?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Arsic, the garrison commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And next to him, beside the --

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Simo Drljaca, MUP chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And do you know who the woman is?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And having a look at this -- this meeting that was being taking place with the ITN reporters, are you able to assist us in where this meeting took place?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Judging by the room I see, it was probably the large meeting hall - that's what we called it - of the Municipal Assembly in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Just fast-forward.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Do you recognise the -- the route that's being taken by this convoy of vehicles?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: We see there a blue APC. Do you recognise that?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just have a look. I can't see it yet. I see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Do you recognise that vehicle?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the armoured vehicle that the police used in Prijedor. We received it from the army, and it was painted blue. It was used for practical purposes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Thank you. That's almost at the end of the tape. And we move on now to another tape which shows the actual visit into Omarska camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: I seek to tender this video at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: If we could have the next video, it's already an exhibit, P1358 -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1623, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, it's tab 48A, the next video. The previous one was 48.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Sir, you see on your screen a line of men in what looks like a canteen. Do you recognise that building?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recognise the building. This is the inside of a building I've never been inside.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Do you recognise any of the men?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. Not for now.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Looking at the -- the general state of condition of the men that we see in this footage, can you comment on whether that -- the men that you saw at Omarska were in a similar state of health or condition to these men?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I cannot, because I don't know them personally. If I had known some of them personally before they were brought here and now -- the way I see them now, then I could comment. But, as it is, I really cannot. This is Simo Drljaca in an office.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: I think that's all we need to do with that video. It's already an exhibit, Your Honours. He can't really comment. He wasn't present at the meeting, so he can't comment on the interactions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm a bit confused. I expected that we would see a video about which this witness would say something and a video after the first one. That's why I -- I didn't object to the first video being admitted, but I don't know what the position of the OTP is about the date of this video and why it is relevant, apart from the fact that the witness identified Simo Drljaca and a couple of people from Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I'm -- Mr. Krgovic, with respect, I'm not sure I follow you. In terms of the second video, the question that was asked was whether the condition of the persons as shown there was what he recalled his own observations to be, and that is items already in evidence. In terms of the first video, it was -- apart from the individuals that he pointed out, it was the path that they -- scenes from the journey to get to the Omarska camp. I'm not sure I follow your reservation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, when introducing the first video, the Prosecutor said, We'll now play the video that this witness discussed. But we haven't seen anything that the witness talked about. I don't understand what is the position of the Prosecutor here. We've seen a convoy of cars with some people in them going somewhere. What's the date of this? Is this the visit that the witness talked about, are these the people? We haven't seen or heard any of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Of course, you would reserve these questions for your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because if that's the position of the Prosecutor, namely, that this was shot when he was there visiting Omarska, then he should be asked about it. That's why I didn't object to the video, the first video, because I expected to see the continuation of the visit, including the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pidwell, do we have a date on which this video has been taken, the first one?

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours. We have a date for the ITN visit when it was first admitted into evidence approximately six months ago, I think. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: That's the second one you mean?

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: That's the second one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes. And the first one?

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: The first one is the -- we don't have a specific date on it, but it was the -- the ITN only went into Omarska once, and that is a video that precedes the second one. It's the Prosecution's case that this video -- these two videos were taken on the same day. One is the unofficial lead-up to Omarska, and the other is taken at Omarska and was part of the broadcast that was aired publicly later on in the year by IN news. The first part of the video wasn't part of that public screening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And what is the date of the second one?

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Second one is early August. Now, it's not the Prosecution's case that this was footage of this man's visit to Omarska, but the purpose of showing Your Honours the first video was the lead-up, and he was able to identify the people who were at the municipal building who were introducing the ITN crew. And the second video was simply to identify Simo Drljaca in that video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Now that the matter has been opened, I'm wondering, Ms. Pidwell, whether we can take your ipse dixit that the first video was -- bears the same date as the second?

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: If Your Honours would like, I can check through the chain of custody for the videos and provide that information to you. If it's an issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Anyway, we -- let's move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I see the transcript records me as saying ipse dicta. It's ipse dixit.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to you show another document, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: It's tab 45. 65 ter 2750.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Sir, you will see on your screen a document dated the 24th of July from the Autonomous Region of Krajina to the Prijedor municipality, confirming a number of decisions which were adopted by the Crisis Staff between 29 May and 24 July, 1992. Were you involved in -- were you involved in making -- or passing these -- making these decisions, firstly, by the Crisis Staff, which were then sent to the -- the Autonomous Region of Krajina to ratify, or were you not involved with those?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I may have an objection to this document. Based on the document, we can see it's a document by the municipality of Prijedor, not by the Autonomous Region of Krajina. I don't see anywhere in the documents, at least in the version that's before us, what decisions of -- no decisions of Autonomous Region of Krajina are mentioned here.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Perhaps I'll ask the witness, then, to explain the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Sir, have you had the opportunity to look at this document?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't had the opportunity to see the document, until the proofing for this trial. Since ARK Krajina had already been formed, in the heading we can see stated Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and Autonomous Region of Krajina, and then Prijedor municipality. All of those were then formed, established by then. And all the municipalities were duty-bound to have all the decisions by their Crisis Staffs verified by the Assembly. This document is related to that. The Assembly verified the decisions of the Crisis Staff. But let me remind you here that presidents of parties and people's deputies were not members of Crisis Staffs, and therefore I'm not familiar with this document. At least I don't have any knowledge of it that stems from that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: All right. We'll leave that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. We would like to hear the explanation by the witness: Who issued the document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe I was clear. It was the Prijedor Municipal Assembly, but because in the memo it is stated that the Republika Srpska will be established and ARK Krajina will be established, the heading reflects that. And then under that it says municipality of Prijedor. And all the decisions made by Crisis Staffs had to be verified by the Assembly. And it was done -- this document was sent to the Assembly, the Assembly then made its decision and verified it. Crisis Staffs took over the role of Assembly because they could not -- the Assemblies could not work during the conflict period, and the idea was to have the Assembly either verify or reject decisions reached by the Crisis Staffs. And it's in this context that we see the subject here, and it's very clear: "Confirmation of decisions within the competence of the Municipal Assembly adopted by the Crisis Staff."

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Well, in light of that explanation, sir, I would ask that the document be admitted or at least MFI'd at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The -- the document may be admitted as an exhibit at this stage.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1624, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to ask you some questions, finally, on the reasons why you attempted to resign from your position in Prijedor in October 1992. Do you recall making -- attempting to resign at that time?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on two occasions. The first time it was in 1992, in the second half of 1992; and the second time was in August 1993, when I stood by this request I submitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And what prompted you to attempt to tender your resignation in the second half of 1992?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the takeover of power, as I've already mentioned during my testimony here and during our previous contacts, so in the period prior to the takeover and during it and up until the attack against Prijedor, there were no incidents in the municipality of Prijedor. After the incidents that did take place - and let me make this clear: I was the president of the party, but the party wasn't functioning at this time - but as a private person I was walking about, and after the armed conflicts in the municipality of Prijedor, there were cases of wilful activity by certain individuals. There were some negative events that took place. And through public discussion, the party seemed to be accused of being behind it. And because of that kind of portrayal of the party among the citizens, which was not correct, I, as the president of the party, for the purpose of defending my own dignity and the dignity of the party, I drafted a document where I explained that in relation to all the negative events that took place in the area of Prijedor that are being ascribed to the party, I submit resignation, unless this document of mine was adopted. And the document had the purpose of washing our hands of all the actions by individuals and groups. And then we also made an appeal to relevant organs to take legal measures against all the people who are involved in illegal activities. But the platform was adopted, and therefore I did not go through with my resignation. Also, the mandate of the people that were part of the structure believed that it's time for younger people to come in and take over. However, since this younger generation also acted wilfully, I then resigned for good. Before that, I had talks with Radovan Karadzic in Mrkonjic Grad, who agreed to my proposals. But on my return, there were obstructions by some people, and I just realized I cannot go on, because I saw that people had same goals. And then I resigned, although the Assembly wasn't there in full complement. On behalf of the Main Board, Mr. Radomir Neskovic was present, and I said, Here you have the representative of the Main Board, but as of today, the 16th of August, I am not the president of the party anymore, and can you formalise that. And that's how things happened.
