utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Sir, you used the phrase "wilful activity of certain individuals and groups." What do you mean by that, and who were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's like this: I can discuss only rumours that were present around Prijedor; namely, it was the party that was blamed for all the activities. But I wanted to defend the party and myself to -- I wanted to prove that it's not correct, and that's why I came up with this document, a platform, a political platform that I presented. I asked for relevant organs to take action. It was their duty to make sure that violations of the law are processed by the police, military police, judiciary. Everything that there were institutions to deal with such issues.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Well, what activities are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: What activities was the party being blamed for at this time?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were talks that they were looting, killing, that they are removing construction material from other people's houses. All the events that come with the war, everything was put on the party's account, so to speak. There were also certain conflicts. But these things, through rumours among the people, created a certain picture of the party. Now, I don't know who was behind that, but the public picture of the party was created in such a manner, and, therefore, I had this published in "Kozarski Vjesnik" so that citizens would know what our position was. You can find it among the documents that are in the possession of the Prosecutor, these "Kozarski Vjesnik" articles.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And when you say that you asked the relevant organs to take action, which organs are you referring to when you make that comment?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you -- is my microphone on? Yes. As I've said, like in any other system, there are institutions such as judiciary, police, military, military police, because we were in a state of war, Military Prosecutor's Offices, all of them had some segments that were in charge of relevant activities. There were cases where individuals were brought in for interrogation, finally even sentenced, through the work of civilian and military police as well. But those who were involved would know better about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And was your complaint that the party was being blamed for the inactions of these municipal organs, or was it something else?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no one I could complain to. Communications were non-existent. Both as the president of the party and as a human being, since our policy was not what was presented, I wanted to show to the citizens what the position really is, my position and the position of the Serbian Democratic Party, so that every citizen would know what our position is.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And which individuals in the municipality did you want replaced?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the set that came to power before the war, Stakic, Mico Kovacevic. I can't remember who else was in the board. And the officials themselves, they were not such a problem, maybe initially; but the police and Simo Drljaca, those were the problems. Simo Drljaca didn't want to step down as the chief. It took some time for that. And only through the assistance of the president of the Assembly, Momcilo Krajisnik, who came to visit to one of the meetings where we were trying to force Drljaca to step down, only then, through his authority, we succeeded in having them replaced.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was in early 1993. The new officials who came in, I remember everything functioned for three months properly with morning briefings as a means of seeing what was done or what wasn't. But then after a while they started acting wilfully and in their own interests, and we tried to replace them. And, finally, I simply had to step down. I think I'm the only one who stepped down. Everybody else was trying to fight to get some political position, but ... maybe I was stupid.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: If Your Honours will just bear with me for one moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Cross-examination -- yes, cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. Miskovic.

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Dragan Krgovic. We've met already.

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I'll be putting questions to you on behalf of Mr. Stojan Zupljanin. But since the two of us speak the same language, before you answer my question, please wait for a while in order to make it possible for the interpreters to interpret what we're saying.

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I believe there was something that you wanted to add at the end of the Prosecutor's questions.

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no, nothing specific. I wanted to say that after I've submitted my request to resign, I also asked to be put back to the position where I was before, but I never received a response. It's just something that got lost in the administration, I guess. Nothing special.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Miskovic, in your direct examination on Friday, you were asked by the Prosecutor about wartime police stations --

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: -- and their organisation. The existence of the wartime police station was something that was pursuant to the Law on Internal Affairs of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did explain that. That was all in keeping with the documentations and laws that were in effect during the existence of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I also said that they were formed in the 1970s than there was training conducted there, both oral and practical. I explained all that, because it involved people who were doing something else, normally. And it was only their wartime assignment that they should have been doing through the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have 1D159 on the screen. It is under tab 6, Zupljanin Defence folder.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you zoom in a little, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: This is a document from 1991 dealing with recruitment and the organisation of the wartime functioning of the MUP. It's a document from the Ministry of Interior, the Socialist Republic.

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the joint authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: It also mentions some sort of unit files that need to be filled in.

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was engaged on the basis of this. I was commander of the reserve police station for three months, because my wartime assignment was to be commander of the reserve police station, and the police force was mixed at the time when I was engaged in 1991, and the police station was called Prijedor 2. So before I withdrew from the position of the commander of the reserve police station to become the president of the party, Prijedor Dva was a mixed police station, and it continued to operate that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: The Prosecutor also asked you about the strength of the police force in Prijedor. You answered that question, and you mentioned the presence of the army in the area of Prijedor. Do you know how many soldiers there were, including the Territorial Defence, in the beginning of 1991 in the area of Prijedor municipality?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know the number of army troops or the police personnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: The Prosecutor also asked you a series of questions about the operation of the municipality on the eve of the conflict. I would like to ask you about the blockade of the work of the Assembly. It was not a result of any SDS action, was it?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I explained that in detail to the Prosecutor. It was the SDA party that prevented the Assembly from operating, and that began even before I became president of the party. When I became president of the party, I named myself head of the committee inquiring into that; and when I did that, within half an hour, we managed to divide up 50 per cent of all the official posts, and the remaining 50 per cent of the posts remained for the next day. However, the SDA leadership blocked the work of this committee, so even this effort was prevented. But I explained all that to the Prosecutor when she asked me. But that was the source of information that I had. It was not second-hand information. I wanted to be briefly at the source to deal with this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: The Prosecutor also asked you about Simo Drljaca and his engagement, if I can call it that, in 1991. You said that he was heading the so-called interest community for education. In 1991, he did not have any official position in the municipality, apart from that, the education part?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: He did not have any entourage, any body-guards, service cars, or anything?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He worked on the education board for secondary and primary education, and he worked together with Mr. Babic. He was on very good terms with him. And he was later recommended by Babic to become a member of the party, and he would be placed in charge of internal supervision within the party. Until then, he had no other position.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about 1991.

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. No, in 1991, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps you didn't understand me. I asked you if he had any body-guards, any security detail, in 1991.

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In 1991, he was just a member of the education board. Even I did not have any other function until 11th September 1991, when I became president of the party.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: The Prosecutor also asked you a series of questions about those meetings of the SDS, starting from the time when you became its president, and you went through these meetings in great detail. Now, in all these talks at these SDS meetings that you chaired, there was no talk at any point, was there, about any violence against Muslims, expelling them, or any discrimination about -- against other ethnicities?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From all I said and from all the documents, it is quite clear that there was not a single statement, not a single action, that would speak to a discriminatory attitude. On the contrary, you will see that through all these events the Serbs were only anxious about preventing the sort of suffering that was inflicted on the Serbs in the past, and that's why we acted to prevent that. And we had constructive talks with all the parties. And we kept repeating - and thank God there are many people still alive who can confirm this - that all our activities were geared at that, avoiding conflict. At one point, I said, Just give me any reason why we should do this. We were afraid of opening old wounds. Many generations by then had grown up together. They were friends, they intermarried, they went to youth labour drives together in major construction projects. And unlike the immediate post-war generation, which still felt those old wounds very bitterly - I don't know if the Trial Chamber knows this, but only from the area of Kozara many civilians ended up in the concentration camp of Jasenovac, and children were placed in a children's concentration camp in Jastrebarsko - that is the old history of which I wanted to give you an overview and you didn't let me. And those were the fears and reasons why we were trying to avoid a new confrontation, to -- we were afraid that all the wounds would be opened and all the achievements in the past 50 years would be ruined. And if you only look at 1967, 1971, 1974, and 1991, you will see that all these events are interconnected. Everything has its cause an effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I have to ask you to slow down a little.

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you have to remind me all the time because I keep forgetting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: One part was not recorded, when you said that the entire Serbian population from Kozara was deported into --

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was their wretched fate. Apart from the people who formed the 1st Partisan Brigade, many civilians remained in their villages and hamlets from Gradiska to Kostajnica. All these civilians ended up in the concentration camp of Jasenovac. The children from Kozara ended up in the Jastrebarsko concentration camp also in Croatia, like Jasenovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Miskovic, will you please slow down. When you were about to tell us about this historical background and all the fears that the old sentiments might be awakened ...

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And that's why it was our policy to do everything possible to prevent a new conflict, a new confrontation, knowing that it was pregnant with consequences.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we show the witness 65 ter 687? It has not been exhibited -- or it has been exhibited, but I don't have the exhibit number. Just a moment, Your Honours, the Prosecutor showed this exhibit some time ago. Sorry, 65 ter 587. P1670, or 17.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You spoke about this a moment ago with the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's from the radio.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see the second page. ERN number is 0100-8950.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: See this paragraph, before the word "reporter," begins with the word "thus." "... that was yet another proof that the middle letter D in the name of our party really means something and that we wanted to eliminate any surprises in this manner. Our intention was to break the ongoing blockade around the division of power and the deliberate drawing of this region into chaos. We had promised that we would not allow these people to be naive and outsmarted for the third time in a row ..." That's what you were saying, that your whole action was geared at --

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Prevention. And this reference to the middle letter D, since it was a democratic party, I want to emphasise that we acted in that spirit, in the spirit of democracy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: The Prosecutor also asked you about the Plan A and Plan B that were part of this action?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was prepared and executed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Now before the walkout of the Serbia deputies from the Assembly, because they were outvoted, the SDS never planned or carried out any actions. Your eventual action was, in fact, a reaction to what was going on in the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everyone knows what happened in the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina. We have already been through this. There was a referendum among the Serbian People concerning a referendum of the Muslims and Croats. No steps had been planned at that point. Everything followed its normal course until the moment when the real danger began to loom that Bosnia-Herzegovina would separate itself from Yugoslavia, and the Serbs were very much against that, very much against a cessation. Than is the main reason why the leadership of the party prepared the Plans A and Plan B, and each of them dealt with a specific scenario. And it says very clearly: In the event of danger, only then would these measures kick in. Otherwise, we would follow a democratic course of action and work normally and take all the steps to achieve a peaceful solution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm not sure, perhaps now is the time for the break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... yes, this is, yes. 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Before Mr. Krgovic resumes, the Chamber is reminded that it has not yet resolved the matter of the -- how much time is going to be needed for the Witness Brown who is scheduled to appear within a little more than a fortnight, and we are wondering whether the parties are in a position at the -- say, within ten minutes, in the last ten minutes of today, to further address us on that question so we know what the -- what is likely to happen. You would appreciate that if any adjustment is going to be made to his appearance, an earlier decision has to be made. In that sense, we would appreciate if the parties are in a position to address us, as I said, about ten minutes before we break today, or, failing that, first thing in the morning. Yes, Mr. Krgovic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Miskovic, let us continue. Just let me, once more, remind you - and that goes for me as well, because I also speak fast - to remind you to slow down.

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, just you remind me occasionally.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Before the break, we discussed the measures taken at the municipal level in Prijedor as a reaction to the events in the Assembly and the down-voting of the deputies of -- of Serb ethnicity in the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina. From the moment you became president of the party and later when you spoke to Mr. Karadzic at these meetings, and I see that you reported to the Municipal Assembly about that, there was never any agreement to take action until the moment when the existence of the Serb People in an area should be endangered; right?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the meetings of the Main Board to which I was invited as president of the party, I can say that there was never talk about intolerance to any other people, and that can be corroborated by the minutes. Never. At no point in time. The reaction of the Serb deputies in the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina was to the aspirations of the other two peoples to bring about the cessation of Bosnia-Herzegovina from Yugoslavia. In that context, the Serb representatives were afraid for the biological survival of the Serb People. And then, as a consequence, a Serb Assembly separated from that Assembly, and then there was also the territorial organisation of the Krajina. That was a period of difficult communication. Later, the procedure was -- and I spoke about Variants A and B. They were the reaction to possible problems that could occur later with regard to the problems connected with the cessation of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the non-acceptance of the Serb People of that cessation and their wish to remain within Yugoslavia. The assessment was probably made in the top echelons of the party that to this could bring about conflict. Then two variants were worked out, and the presidents of the Municipal Boards were to act in accordance, when the survival of the Serb People in their municipality would be in danger. And it was explained in that context.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You said, Mr. Miskovic, that one of the decisions of the Serb People in the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina to carry out a plebescite about remaining in Yugoslavia; right?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because of the decision of the Serb representatives to separate from the work of the Assembly for the reasons stated, namely, the wish of the other two peoples to bring about the cessation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that's why the decision was adopted -- or could you repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I asked you about the plebescite of the Serb People.

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to check what the Serb People felt, whether they would back it up, they -- there was a -- so there was a plebescite which was conducted by means of which the opinion or the attitude of the Serb People was checked, whether they wanted to secede or remain within Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Answering the Prosecutor's question with regard to the intercepted conversation with Mr. Tadic [as interpreted], you said that in the territory of Prijedor municipality, 60 per cent of the population are Serbs and that this information differs from the information contained in the results of the census in 1991?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's a fact. But you must bear in mind that after the official census, the share of the ethnicities was inadequate, because 8 per cent of the population stated that they were Yugoslavs. And out of these 8 per cent, 80 to 90 per cent were actually Serbs. Bearing in mind that fact, I said before that the actual situation was not as reflected in the census results. But this new census which was carried out by going from house to house actually confirmed these assumptions that Prijedor had a Serb majority, and I informed the president of the party accordingly, and I pointed out to them the newly -- the new situation, based on the newly established state of affairs. And I had my people check whether the constitution allowed for additional steps. So nothing was done rashly, if this is enough.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Just one intervention in the transcript: It records Mr. Krgovic stating at line -- page 58 line 1: "There was an intercepted conversation with Mr. Tadic." And I'm just wondering if you could clarify that because I didn't play him any conversations with Mr. Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Miskovic, what I asked you about, I spoke about intercepted conversations with Mr. Karadzic; correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I explained as much to the OTP. And I explained once more in detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And further on in that intercepted conversation, Simovic is mentioned. Do you remember the position of Mr. Simovic at that time, the vice-prime minister?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. But I know that he was a lawyer, and that's why I tasked him with these things, because he knows these things. It is his field of expertise, and I wanted him to provide answers. So we wanted to check whether it was possible under the constitution and laws and regulations whether this was possible, and the right man to do that was Simovic. And it will be clear to anybody who reads through that. Of course, I mean the one reading these texts must be a -- an expert, not a layperson. And I don't know which position he held.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: The Prosecutor asked you a series of questions about the shadow cabinet which was established at one point. As far as I understood your answer, this appointment of people, the Crisis Staff and -- or to call it the shadow cabinet, was no secret. There were even jokes among Muslims and Serbs because everybody knew who was in witch position; right?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was half-public and half-secret, but hardly anything was hidden. I can only speak about what I took part in. We really wanted to find adequate solutions. But we also stated clearly: Where we couldn't come up with an adequate solution, we would have to provide a reserve solution. And that was Variant B, which was in force for Prijedor municipality. It was, again, in line with the instructions that were in effect for all municipalities in Bosnia and Herzegovina. And about jokes, yes, there were jokes around. I like to -- I'm detached from everything. That's my nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And this shadow cabinet, was -- its existence was used in talks with the SDA. You said to them that unless a solution is found that you will establish this shadow cabinet?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we didn't speak to them about that. We only said that a solution to all the problems in and around Prijedor must be found. We went into the relations that existed formally about all the traumas, and they knew all that. But only -- I only reminded them of that, to have everybody understand that things were serious so that the problems about which I have already spoken today should not aggravate. And I said that people intermarried, they worked together, and so on and so forth. So there were friendships in place and very good relations, partly. So in order to avoid destroying all that, and for the young generation who haven't lived through the Second World War and didn't have any blood on their hands, should be spared of -- of chaos once more in history.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know if the Muslim side, the SDA, had any plans of their own, something like your Variants A and B?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say that with certainty because I'm not acquainted with their plans, but I know I heard from military circles that they have units ready, that they are arming themselves, that they have weapons. That's what I heard. But I never heard as much from them. It isn't any -- it isn't the information that I received directly from the other side. At the time, I thought that military security knew everything, that they were on top of it all. And, actually, they were, because they had their informants in all ethnic groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I understood you, you didn't hear from the Muslim side that they have all that, but you got all that information from the army, that there are such plans and such units and so on?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I didn't receive information directly, through my contacts. But I did hear it from military representatives that they are armed. Actually, both sides. And that they have snipers, both sides, actually. And all citizens had heard of it. And that some people would be slaughtered, this day and other, on the following day. But this isn't anything that I was in a position to know even then, let alone today, after 20 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Just a correction to the transcript: When you said that they had their structures and their weapons, you were referring to the Muslim and the Croat side; right?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. But I did say that the man Slavko Ecimovic commanded one of those units, the Green Berets. He was a Croat, but he commanded a Muslim unit. I sent Dr. Sadikovic to inform him that I wanted to talk to him so that nothing silly happens. Afterward when he was taken prisoner and I asked Zeljaja to talk to him, which was approved, and I asked him what came into him and what he had done, he only answered, Well, I know you, and I know what are you like. Well, he should have listened to me when I first spoke to him, but possibly my assumptions were not altogether correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: On page 63, line 16, it was entered in the transcript to -- that you're referring to two sides, and I just wanted to make clear that the two sides you meant were the Muslims and the Croats.

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Miskovic, you mentioned in your testimony the date when you left to go to the meeting at the SJB of Prijedor on the 29th of April and that there was a problem with an order that arrived at the station.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see Exhibit 1D150. That is tab - let me just see - tab 5 of the Zupljanin Defence binder.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the microphone of the accused please be switched off.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us enlarge ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's a document issued by Delimustafic. And we can see here that the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina made a decision - and then several paragraphs - that complete and massive roadblocks shall be set up along all roads on which JNA units are expected to pull out. And then item 2: "Block the wider surroundings of military facilities from which materiel and equipment are likely to be taken out and -- and they shall be guarded by the units of the TO of the Republic of BH and the MUP." And 3: "Unannounced convoys of former JNA units and convoys without MUP escort shall not be allowed to leave the barracks or communicate within the territory of the Republic BH." And under 4: "Accelerate planning and start combat activities on the entire territory of the Republic of BiH and coordinate these with the TO staff of the region, the district, and the Republic of BiH." And it goes on to speak about the protection of the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: This is what basically arrived at the SJB, something with this content, that MUP units shall be blocked and that preparations for fighting JNA units that were starting to pull out of BiH shall be launched?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read this order, and what I can say is that at the meeting that I attended that took place within the premises of Prijedor MUP and where Mirza Mujadzic, SDA president, was also present, and the president of the municipality whose name I keep forgetting but it's Muhamed Cehajic, a man who was the communicating officer -- a communications officer within MUP Prijedor arrived with a dispatch and he stood there in the middle of the room and read out the dispatch to all of us. Present there were all police members, in other words, this was mixed police complement, and we all suddenly gasped because there we are discussing issues and then suddenly there is a very explicit, direct order, with tasks specified. And there were already experiences from Slovenia and Croatia where soldiers were withdrawing from barracks, and images, let's say, from Split, where a soldier who it later turned out was a Macedonian was being strangled in a tank. It was a shock for all of us. It took us a few seconds before things sort of settled down, and then there was commotion among us officers there. Discussions started breaking out. But, in short, we managed to conclude this meeting. I, at the time, had no idea - nobody had who was present there - that something like this can be expected. However, when we received the dispatch, it was a signal to us that something must be done in order to prevent escalation and to prevent uncontrolled behaviour of either individuals or groups. And, fortunately, at least for that period of time, the takeover of power succeeded in stopping conflicts in Prijedor. The situation was calm until the 30th of May, when the Muslim forces attempted, again, to attack Prijedor, after crossing the Sana River, and changing the situation there. The shooting ensued, Slavko Ecimovic was arrested, and, as I've mentioned, later on, I talked with him in the barracks. But that's how things started. And, yes, this caused all the meetings and activation of Variant B. I already explained that while the OTP was putting questions to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Let me show you another document, Mr. Miskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have 1D151. That's Zupljanin Defence binder, tab --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters failed to hear the tab number. Apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is tab 8. Can we please enlarge this for the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I forgot to add: The signature in the previous document, it said Delimustafic, but I was told at the time it was Doko, Jerko Doko. But the essence of the dispatch is not in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's see this enlarged, please, because I want to see -- oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it has been enlarged.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: What I read to you and the document, the content, is it -- it's identical, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: There is a document in front of you, commander of BH army, Colonel Hasan Efendic signed, where Mr. Doko was the minister. It's the identical content of this document and the document I had shown you before by Delimustafic?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, it's the same request. Maybe it is the same because this was a decision by the BH Presidency. They were the authority. At least they should have been the authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: When you mean the Presidency, you mean the rump Presidency?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's why the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina was established, that's why the plebescite was held, that's why the Variants B and B were drafted, precisely in order to make sure that such unpredictable things would not happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise, my question is not on the record. What I said was: This was without Serb representatives. It's the rump Presidency without the Serb representatives?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the situation at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Miskovic, after attending the meeting with the president -- with the representatives of the police and the army, they also knew about the dispatch that there was order to enter the conflict against JNA; they knew about it, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I know that upon my arrival I was shown this, and during the conversations with the prosecutor's office in Sarajevo I was shown a dispatch that arrived one day prior about which I didn't know anything also --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You didn't understand me. When you received the information and when you went to the meeting with Serb representatives up there in the barracks, then you informed them about it, or did they already know about it?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They all knew about it. I -- I was the only one who didn't know. They knew about it. They were all up there. It was only me missing, and then I came. Everybody was already seated up there in the barracks. Arsic, Zeljaja, Simo, Kuruzovic, all of them. The leadership. Stakic also.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And it was at that meeting that the assessment was made that the situation has reached a crucial moment, that something has to be done in order to prevent conflicts, avoid conflicts with the other side?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The main reason for the takeover of power was precisely that; namely, the suggestions that one could see in this dispatch. And that's how it was explained at the time. The decision was reached because of that, to take over the power, deadlines made for final decisions, assignments made for Territorial Defence and police for the takeover of power and for the purpose of preventing the activities that one can find enumerated in the dispatch. That was the reason. Up until that moment, it was only on paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: It was an autonomous decision reached by the representatives of the Serbian People in the municipality of Prijedor. You didn't get any instructions from the leadership of the party or from the leadership otherwise. It was a decision reached at the local level, and it was prompted by the said events?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no. Nothing was reached independently. You knew -- you know about the existence of Variants B and A. So the Territorial Defence had been formed. We knew who was at the head of the Territorial Defence and MUP. We made sure that we can prevent any threat to the Serbian People in the area. It applied to all the municipalities, not only to Prijedor. Since these threats existed in the dispatch, we have acted in accordance with Variant B, namely, doing anything that's necessary to prevent violence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: But you -- you didn't get a specific instruction on the 30th or around that date: You need to do such and such a thing.

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. We just activated what existed on paper already. Because the conditions were fulfilled with the arrival of the dispatch, showing that there was a threat in the municipality of Prijedor. This is not a threat only to the Serbian People, according to my reading. We were the representative of the Serbian People, yes, but our goal was to prevent any confrontation and to prevent tragedy for all the ethnic groups in the area. And it functioned for 30 days until the attack against Prijedor. There were no incidents, no conflicts, nothing. Like in any town, there were Muslim and Croats' bars and other shops in Prijedor that were not touched. One can prove that. But later on, there was an escalation which had its consequences. But that's a different story.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Just one more question related to this: Do you know that one of the results of this dispatch in the territory of the, let's say, Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina was ordered to mobilize the reserve police forces and putting them under combat readiness?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By whom?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, on both sides. Both parties ordered reserve police stations to be mobilized.

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that, on the 29th of April --

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah, the day before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: -- that it was ordered that the full police complement should be mobilized, not only in the municipality of Prijedor but in all Krajina municipalities?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I thought I explained it. I may not have been clear enough. We acted according to Variant B, to Plan B, which involves every municipality in Bosnia. And individual municipalities made assessments according to their needs. Everything was regulated on paper, but no measures were taken before there was an obvious threat. And once the threat was obvious, measures were taken to prevent tragedy in the area, in this specific case, in the municipality of Prijedor. But it was -- the same applied for all municipalities that were within the B Variant conditions as well as for the other, for the A Variant conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: On that day, on the 29th of April, when you were in the Prijedor SJB, Hasan Telundzic, was still there?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was still presiding the meeting there as the chief of MUP. He was presiding the meeting. The rest of us were guests; myself, Mirza Mujadzic as the SDA president, and president of the Municipal Assembly, Muhamed Cehajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Prosecutor also showed you document P652.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please put that up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Drljaca, who, at the time, already took over as the chief, he is here sending to the Banja Luka CSB a dispatch containing, let's say, two information. The first one is that ten police stations with 1.587 policemen were mobilized.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And, second, no one failed to respond or avoided work duty. That's the first part of the dispatch. And in the second part it is stated that in accordance with the conclusion of the Executive Board of the Serbian Assembly of Prijedor municipality, control was seized over facilities. And then there's an explanation of how it took place.

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: We can see "in reference to," and your dispatch, and then there's a number. It's in reference to a dispatch issued on 29th of April. But you haven't seen that?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't know anything about that, but it's related to the issue of the takeover of power and other problems. But I didn't know. It was difficult for me to find this out, when I found out about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: There's another -- there's a dispatch that I'm going to show you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is document 2D-1943. It's tab 7 of the Zupljanin binder. I apologise, 2D02-1943. I apologise, 2D03-1943.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please enlarge this for me? It's rather illegible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please enlarge this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: This is a dispatch sent to all the security stations, to all, to the chief, on the 29th of April --

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I'm sorry, but my -- the English version states that it is sent to the security stations in Bosanski Petrovac, Bosansko Grahovo, Drvar, Kupres, Teslic. It doesn't necessarily say to all of the SJBs in the area of the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It must be a language problem. It says SJB, that is, public security station, to all, to the chief, and then it names other separate addressees in the second line.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please look, Witness, tell us, whether it says: SJB, to all, to the chief, and then individual SJBs are named.

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says clearly: "... public security station - to all - to the chief." And then in the second line, it says, again: "Public security service, Bosanski Petrovac, Bosansko Grahovo, Drvar, Kupres, Teslic, to the chief." "To the president ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not interested in the presidents of these Serbian municipalities that are named.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Ms. Pidwell, are you satisfied that we are looking at the same document?

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: I am satisfied that we're looking at the same document. I'm not satisfied that the meaning of the words is what is being portrayed. But it may be a matter of interpretation and the wondering of the Serbian version as well as the English. I can't really assist because I don't understand the nuances between the languages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can make it clearer with the help of the witness, although we've already heard evidence about this. When it says "SJB - to all," it means that it's addressed to all the public security stations in the area of -- of a CSB.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Miskovic, at the time when you were working as a policeman, when you would receive a dispatch from the centre of security services and when it's addressed "SJB - to all," does that mean to all the public security stations under the supervision of that centre?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, to all those covered by the sender.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And these stations, Bosanski Petrovac, Bosansko Grahovo, Drvar, Kupres, Teslic, at the time, they were not under the CSB Banja Luka. They only joined later, and that's why they are named separately?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that. I can't tell you anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: If you don't know, I won't insist. Mr. Zupljanin repeats here, although we can only see that the signature says "Chief" but we don't if he really signed it. Anyway, this dispatch repeats the order sent by Delimustafic. It says, in the introduction, the minister of the interior of the Republic of BH reference, et cetera, et cetera, and then Delimustafic's dispatch is literally rendered.

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It begins, I think, on page 1, and then continues on page 2. Here it says: "Speed up plan and begin combat activities."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Now, regarding this dispatch, on the following page you see the measures recommended by the CSB, the Security Services Centre. Look at page 2.

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 2 in Serbian. And could we zoom in on the first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can hardly see. "Carry out a full and comprehensive mobilization of the active-duty and reserve police force and all the other employees in public security stations."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: So one of the measures ordered by the CSB is to carry out a full and comprehensive mobilization of the active-duty and reserve police and all the other employees in public security stations. In item 2, it says: "Go for full combat readiness." Can we now go back to 5652.

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean those provisional measures?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I meant P652.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Drljaca says here ten police stations have been mobilized. He indicates their strength. And there were no cases of non-response. So this is the request for mobilization, the order for mobilization that arrived on Telundzic's desk?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't be very sure. I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Miskovic, I'm asking you these questions precisely because you said you were confused when the Prosecutor showed you these dispatches. And since you hadn't seen the dispatch on which the reply of Mr. Drljaca was based, I wanted to show you this dispatch to which Drljaca was actually replying. It concerns the full mobilization of all the police complements of all public security stations in the territory of the centre. That's the dispatch from the 29th.

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. When I saw reference, dispatch dated 28th April, I was sorry I wasn't informed about it. And I realized when I came to that meeting in the barracks that everybody was already very well informed. I was the only one who was not privy to it. And I still feel left out after 13 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: It's just missing from the record that when -- you meant when you saw this dispatch from Delimustafic that the -- the contents is the same?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter does not understand the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I will ask you a leading question to deal with this. When you are saying that you were not aware of these dispatches, you are talking about Doko's dispatch or, rather, Delimustafic's dispatch that was just shown to you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as Doko's dispatch is concerned, I knew about it, I was there when it was read out at the meeting at the police. Now, who signed it, I don't know. I knew all the time that it was from Doko, and I thought it was the dispatch related to the previous period. And it was very hard for me to feel that I am out of the loop. Everyone else was informed. I was the only one who didn't know about it. After so many years, I still feel left out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Miskovic, you described that the takeover was peaceful, and, at that time, on the 30th of April and in the days that followed, there were no skirmishes, there were no armed clashes until the moment of the attack.

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only armed skirmishes. There were no verbal clashes either, as I explained here in the courtroom. I met with Cehajic, who was president of the municipality until then. I talked to him. He was unhappy, but still, we had a normal conversation. I tried to present my arguments and reasons. He was unable to accept them. His vanity was hurt. And I can understand all that. But, at any rate, I thought then that our solution was much more painless, and it really was, until the attack on Prijedor on the 30th of May. There was no incident, no verbal clash, no armed incident. Nothing. Until the attack on Prijedor. You can see that from the documents. You can see that if you speak to people from the area of all ethnicities. There was no conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Then continuing to reply to the Prosecutor's questions, you talked about the talks with the representatives of Kozarac, and you mentioned your involvement in those negotiations. You mentioned some other participants. Those were talks at the local level, in Prijedor; right?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These talks were held at the level of the municipality of Prijedor, and the basic purpose was as I described: To find jointly some solutions to avoid confrontation, because, as I saw it, there was no reason for confrontation in the municipality. And I told them, Give me one reason why we should have a conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And there was nobody from the outside, outside Prijedor, at those talks?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We dealt with it on our own. It was our problem. We were looking for solutions. We thought we would find solutions in contacts with people, in talks. Even before the takeover I had tried to establish these contacts, because the Assembly was unable to meet, because it was paralysed, because tensions were rising. I asked my Muslim deputy to go and talk to people, to defuse tensions, to avoid conflicts. However, he shirked from that all the time, and I asked him straightforwardly, How come that I have the courage to go to Muslim communities and you don't have the courage to go to Serb communities? I can only assume that we were briefed differently. We had been given different platforms. My only aim was to avoid that -- that the fate of the Serbian People from 1914 and 1941 not repeat itself. That was the main motivation of my generation, all the people who were born in 1945, like me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Part of your answer does not seem to be on record.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: The last bit, when you said that the wounds were still fresh, that you are the generation of 1945. That part is missing. Mr. Miskovic, you had a special interest in -- in keeping peace in -- in those talks in Kozarac because you spent part of your youth in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My general commitment at that time and always is to have a peaceful conversation with every individual, every group, anyone who could contribute to a peaceful solution. I know it's difficult from this perspective to understand what kind of times these were, but by that time we had seen wars in Croatia, in Slovenia, the psychology of killing, it was a general psychoses that everyone lived in their own way. And at that time, in order to avoid the repetition of 1941 and the concentration camps and the concentration camps for children and the massacres on Kozara Mountain, to avoid putting salt and reopening these old wounds and to preserve all that has been achieved -- had been achieved over the 50 years in terms of mutual peaceful co-existence with all the mixed marriages, the mixed friendships. And a member of my family, one of my brothers-in-law, is a Muslim. I spent my childhood there, of course, but I had also tried, through my commander, to do the same in his local area. I brought their people through the check-points to talk together. Kadinic [phoen] always said it's not the right time. Maybe now he can explain why it was not the right time. To me, it was always the right time. And you can see it from all of my actions and all my words.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I see the witness is very emotional at the moment. I think he's crying. Perhaps we should adjourn now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's very difficult for me to talk about these things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, I agree, Mr. Krgovic. Thank you. Mr. Miskovic, we -- your testimony obviously is not complete, but we are near the time where we would adjourn for the day. We have some administrative matters with which to deal, so I'm going to excuse you at this point, and we will resume tomorrow morning at 9.00. The usher will escort you from the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'm really sorry I got so emotional.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Ms. Pidwell, are you or other counsel from the OTP present in court able to assist us further with the timing question which was raised by Mr. Zecevic who, of course, is not with us today. But you -- you were present in court, if memory serves, and you remember his concerns. And we had invited a response from the OTP and, as I said, we had left the matter unresolved. Are you in a position - when I say you, I mean "you" plural - in a position to speak to this at this moment?

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, Your Honours. My understanding was -- where it was left was to work out the length of time it would take for Mr. Brown to conclude his evidence in-chief and cross-examination. He is -- on the timings that I have, we have estimated four hours as evidence in-chief and I have a total of seven and a half hours of cross-examination estimates provided by the Defence. So I've put him in the schedule for three full days in the week commencing the 18th of October. And as -- as previously discussed, I think when this was raised last week, I advised that he -- he would start and finish within that week and then -- and that was the only week that he was available, within this calendar year. The -- the issue that Mr. Zecevic raised about not being in a position to cross-examine him because of the disclosure of the Mladic audios, I think I addressed that fully last week, when I advised that the disclosure had taken place, and the only portions of the disclosure which fell within Rule 66 (B) were two audios and one video, which had been identified from the masses of -- of material specifically asked for by the Defence and provided by us, together with the summary of all of the contents of those materials. So that information was provided to them together with a summary and the identification of what audios and videos fell within the parameters of 66 (B), namely, those three individual items, and was -- the summary was provided on the basis that they have asked for this information. We didn't feel a need to disclose it under any of the Rules because in our view it wasn't relevant. But in doing so, we would provide to them -- and we highlighted the fact that it should not be relied upon for the grounds for an adjournment, in order to review. Because, as I've said, it doesn't fall within the ambit of the Rules, and it is not a matter -- it is not material that is relevant to the cross-examination of Mr. Brown. The material that is relevant has been specifically identified and, as I said, is only confined to three tapes. So it's the Prosecution position that he should be called as scheduled. It will create immense problems in terms of the all other witnesses which had been scheduled for the period of October and November - and Your Honours are aware that we have really tightly scheduled them in order to get through them by the end of November - if he is unable to on that day. Because from -- it's only two weeks away, and we're unlikely to fill that position if we can't bring him, because we're going to have to reshuffle all of the ones that are coming up thereafter. And, as I've said, they have been meticulously scheduled in order that we don't have any breaks and that we can finish before the end of November.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Worst case, Ms. Pidwell, we start with him on the 18th and the counsel for Stanisic is in fact not able to complete his cross-examination within the time projected, where do we go from there?

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Well, in that week, sir, if it's not able to be completed, we would be looking for extra sessions that week to conclude his testimony. Because within that -- if they -- within the cross-examination estimates provided to us, we will be able to complete him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Ms. Pidwell, was Ewan Brown supposed to begin his testimony on the 18th or on the 20th?

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: On the 20th I have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: On the 20th of October --

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: That's right. The Wednesday, Thursday, Friday of that week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And we are sitting mornings that week. And we had anticipated that if it looked like we would go over, then we would ask for extra sessions that week to conclude him at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And am I right to also establish that the Prosecution had asked for two hours' examination-in-chief and that the cross-examination of Mr. Zecevic was scheduled to last five hours and by Mr. Krgovic two and a half hours, all together nine and a half hours; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: That was the original estimate provided when we had sought to have his evidence tendered pursuant to 92 ter. You may -- Your Honours may recall in August last year when we had [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... yes, yes, but I'm referring to the batting order which was delivered to us on the 1st of October --

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... and as I have been advised by Ms. Korner, who is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So what are the right figures?

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: It's four hours for the Prosecution and the Defence. Those were the -- those were the estimates provided to us by the Defence. Five plus two and a half.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So this is all together 11 and a half hours?

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Will we be able to realistically, even with extended sittings on Wednesday, Thursday, and Friday, to complete this testimony by the end of Friday?

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Well, we're hoping that he -- we may be able to bring him up earlier, so -- I mean, he is here from the weekend. So whenever the previous witness finishes, he will start.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with all due respect, I believe that this assessment of the OTP is unrealistic, especially considering who is scheduled to come and testify in that week. There is a protected witness who is a military professional and whose examination-in-chief is not completed. It was Ms. Korner who examined him. So that our assessments are much less conservative. And with regard to the testimony of Expert Witness Brown, I'm not sure that we will stay with our estimate of two and a half hours, at least as far as the Zupljanin Defence is concerned, because due to all the current issues still pending, we have not made our final estimate yet. I agree that a possible solution would be to have the witness complete the examination-in-chief and then shift the cross-examination. I believe that it's unrealistic to assess that the end of the Prosecution case will be in November because we are well behind the original estimate of the OTP even now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, do you take issue with the Prosecution's submission that what you have to deal with in relation to the testimony by Dr. Brown is only three tapes? I mean, if that is correct, it doesn't seem to be insurmountable, does it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we haven't had the chance to see the entire material. What the OTP consider relevant for them may not be relevant for us. We cannot tell you. But speaking about the expert witness, let me say that in that huge bulk of material that was disclosed at the beginning of the trial, right now we have now come as far as tab 147, and we believe that there is sufficient material, apart from Mladic's diaries and cassettes, a huge amount of material that was disclosed to us in the meantime. And because the trial is ongoing and we sit every day, we were also unable to review it all. And for -- also for the reasons mentioned by Mr. Zecevic, I believe that it is preferable to have the testimony of Mr. Brown shifted toward the end of the OTP case or, at least, enable us to conduct the cross-examination at that time. I would like to remind you of the testimony of Expert Witness Nielsen. It was extended greatly, and all deadlines were -- all deadlines were crossed, were -- so I believe that the OTP's assessment or estimate is unrealistic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic, do you have anything to add briefly before we take the adjournment? Because we have past the 1.45 mark.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. The Stanisic Defence's position is unchanged. My learned friend has put forward valid arguments to further the extension of the deadline to examine the expert witness, and the Defence position is unchanged in this regard. And as for Mr. Krgovic's submission, I would like to add that the relevance and the scope of the material is for the Defence to assess. So it's for us to decide what's relevant for us and how much time we'll need to deal with it. I'm sure that you will agree with me when I say that the testimony of this expert witness has aroused much interest, both on the part of the OTP and on the part of the Defence. So we stand by our position that the examination of the expert witness be postponed until the end of the OTP case. Or, alternatively, to have the examination-in-chief as scheduled and then have the cross-examination shifted toward the end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Ms. Pidwell, is there any chance of his returning for cross-examination in the new year?

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution -- if Your Honours rule that we can't schedule him for that week in October, we would prefer to have his entire evidence, examination-in-chief and cross-examination, conducted at one time. And as I previously advised, if we finish, as scheduled, towards the end of November, we would then have to break and bring him in the new year because he is unavailable to travel at any other time in this current calendar year, besides that week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. We take the adjournment to tomorrow at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 5th day of October, 2010, at 9.00 a.m. 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
